Sacrificial Ledger.fam: Schema-therapy domain placement, not an owner-dictated clinical filing: Other- Directedness with resentment (canon.json's own I-tagged note). A trait/schema description, not a diagnosis. Canon-asserted member of registers.hyper_complexes[7], 'Persecutory Collapse' (tag I, HiTOP internalizing spectrum, distress subfactor), alongside Collapse and Abandonment Reactivity (both Batch 2) -- see flag above.
Sacrificial Ledger.def: Giving to another person past the point of genuine willingness, while privately tracking what has been given and expecting it to be recognized or returned -- the giving functions as a claim on the other person, not an act closed on its own terms.
Sacrificial Ledger.body: Martyr supplies the sustained sadness and felt deprivation of chronic over-giving. Victim supplies the sense of being wronged when the giving goes unacknowledged or unreturned. Enabler supplies the behavioral delivery mechanism: continuing to give, absorb, or smooth over, even once resentment has already set in, because withdrawing the giving feels as costly as the giving itself. Young's own account of the Self- Sacrifice schema names this exact sequence directly: giving that leaves one's own needs unmet, which turns into resentment of the very people being cared for.
Sacrificial Ledger.inferenceBasis: The name, saboteur triad and schema-domain placement are canon.json's own system-inferred entry (tag I), not owner dictation and not my own invention. The behavioral template below draws on three separately real literatures: Young's Self-Sacrifice schema specifically (not the domain as a whole), Helgeson and Fritz's unmitigated communion, and classical equity theory's account of distress under a relationship felt as unfair. All three saboteurs code to the same engine family (Collapse) per SAB_LIB, so this complex is not blocked from a live reading by the family-spanning mechanism that blocks two other records in this batch.
Sacrificial Ledger.behavior: May give time, money, care or attention well past the point of comfortable willingness, track what has been given even when it is never said aloud, and experience a flare of resentment or injury when the giving is not noticed, thanked, or reciprocated in kind -- while continuing the same pattern of giving afterward rather than reducing it.
Sacrificial Ledger.triggerMechanism: An opportunity to help, placate, or give can activate giving past one's own actual willingness, driven by guilt at attending to one's own needs first. The other person's failure to notice, thank, or reciprocate can separately activate resentment, which does not reliably reduce the future giving -- the ledger keeps running rather than closing the account by giving less.
Sacrificial Ledger.livedExample: A person repeatedly covers for a partner's or family member's shortfall -- money, time, emotional labor -- without being asked to stop, and says nothing about it directly. When the shortfall is not acknowledged, the person feels wronged and may raise old instances of giving in an unrelated argument, while the pattern of covering continues afterward unchanged.
Sacrificial Ledger.impact: The relationship accrues an unspoken debt that only one party is keeping track of, so the other party cannot reciprocate what they do not know is owed, and ordinary disagreements can get loaded with old, unspoken grievances about past giving. Real research on unmitigated communion links this pattern to worse health outcomes for the person doing the giving, not only relational strain.
Sacrificial Ledger.practice: State what you are giving and what you need in return, out loud, before giving it, rather than tracking it silently and expecting it to be read. When resentment appears, treat it as a signal to reduce or renegotiate the giving itself, not only as a feeling to manage. Separate what you are actually willing to give from what guilt is pushing you to give.
Sacrificial Ledger.oppositeDefinition: Settled giving: giving within one's own actual willingness, stating needs and expectations rather than tracking them silently, and treating an unreciprocated pattern as a reason to renegotiate it rather than a debt to carry forward unspoken.

Exploitation.def: Using other people instrumentally to secure an advantage: shaping what they believe or know to get what is wanted, pursuing that aim without being checked by its cost to them, and relocating responsibility for the resulting harm once it becomes visible.
Exploitation.body: Manipulator supplies deliberate management of what another person believes or knows, in the service of a wanted outcome. Aggressor supplies pursuit of that outcome without the ordinary check of weighing the cost to the other person. Deflector supplies the follow-on move once harm becomes visible: relocating responsibility for it rather than owning it. Canon's own note names this precisely: manipulativeness, deceitfulness and callousness are three of the PID-5 Antagonism domain's six named facets (alongside attention seeking, grandiosity and hostility), confirmed across all three prior batches' own use of this same domain.
Exploitation.inferenceBasis: The name, saboteur triad and PID-5 domain placement are canon.json's own system-inferred entry (tag I), not owner dictation and not my own invention. The behavioral template below draws on the PID-5 Antagonism domain (Krueger et al., 2012, reused from all three prior batches' own verification of it), the Dark Triad literature (Paulhus & Williams, 2002), and DSM-5's own 'interpersonally exploitative' narcissism criterion, which gives this complex's name a direct clinical-language anchor none of the other four records in this batch has. The D-factor claim in the hyper-complex row this complex belongs to is named above but explicitly excluded from this record's own confidence basis, because I could not verify its specific number.
Exploitation.behavior: May shape what another person believes or is told specifically to secure a wanted outcome, pursue that outcome without being checked by how much it costs the other person, and, once the resulting harm is visible to others, explain it in a way that relocates responsibility rather than owning it directly.
Exploitation.triggerMechanism: A situation where a wanted outcome depends on another person's belief, consent or choice can activate shaping what that person is told. A perceived obstacle or cost to someone else, once the outcome is already in motion, does not reliably stop the pursuit of it. Visible harm, once it can no longer be hidden, can activate relocating responsibility for it.
Exploitation.livedExample: A person withholds or reshapes information specifically so that someone else agrees to something they would not have agreed to with the full picture. When the gap becomes apparent and causes real harm, the explanation offered attributes the outcome to the other person's own choices or to circumstances, not to the information that was withheld.
Exploitation.impact: Erodes the other party's capacity for informed consent in the relationship, and once the pattern is recognized, trust does not return easily -- people who have been exploited this way tend to withdraw good faith pre-emptively from then on, which can then be read by the person doing the exploiting as confirming that others cannot be trusted either.
Exploitation.practice: Before shaping what someone else is told, name explicitly what information is being withheld and why. Weigh the actual cost to the other person as a real constraint on the outcome, not an afterthought to manage if it surfaces. When harm becomes visible, name your own role in it before naming anyone else's or any circumstance's.
Exploitation.oppositeDefinition: Respected agency: giving others the real information their choices depend on, weighing the cost to them as a genuine constraint on a wanted outcome rather than an obstacle to manage, and owning one's own role in resulting harm rather than relocating it.

Standard Enforcement.def: Holding other people to an exacting standard of correctness, and treating their shortfall against that standard as something to be punished or shamed rather than simply corrected -- the standard and the punishment for missing it are both aimed outward, at other people, rather than inward at the self.
Standard Enforcement.body: Perfectionist and Stickler together supply the exacting standard itself: devotion to one correct way of doing things and to flawless execution. Judge supplies the punitive turn once someone else falls short of it -- moral or critical condemnation, not neutral correction. Where Rigidity (Batch 2) pairs the same two standard-setting saboteurs with Hyper-Vigilant and keeps the pattern largely self-directed, this complex keeps the standard-setting pair and swaps in Judge, which is what turns the same exacting standard outward onto other people, exactly as the shell's own closing phrase, 'pointed outward,' states.
Standard Enforcement.inferenceBasis: The name, saboteur triad and schema-domain placement are canon.json's own system-inferred entry (tag I), not owner dictation and not my own invention. The behavioral template below draws on Hewitt and Flett's other-oriented perfectionism (a real, separately measured dimension of their own Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale, distinct from self-oriented and socially-prescribed perfectionism), Young's Unrelenting Standards and Punitiveness schemas, and the real, verified CAD-triad literature on contempt as a specifically other-directed moral emotion.
Standard Enforcement.behavior: May hold other people to a standard of correctness the person applies inconsistently to themselves, respond to someone else's shortfall with visible disapproval or moral framing rather than neutral correction, and show frustration or conflict specifically when others fail to meet expectations the person has set for them.
Standard Enforcement.triggerMechanism: Observing another person's work, conduct or choice fall short of an internally held standard can activate a punitive response -- contempt-adjacent disapproval rather than plain feedback -- especially where the shortfall is framed as a character failing ('careless,' 'not serious about this') rather than a simple error.
Standard Enforcement.livedExample: A colleague's or family member's work does not meet the standard the person expects. The response is not limited to naming what is wrong with the work -- it carries visible disapproval of the person for having produced it, delivered in a way that reads as judgment of their character rather than feedback on the task.
Standard Enforcement.impact: People around the person learn to anticipate punitive judgment rather than correction, which can suppress honest reporting of mistakes and shift effort toward avoiding visible failure rather than toward the actual standard. The relationship organizes around meeting or dodging the standard rather than around the work itself.
Standard Enforcement.practice: Before responding to someone else's shortfall, separate the correction itself from any judgment of their character. Apply the same standard to your own work that you are applying to theirs, and say so out loud when you do. Offer the correction without the punitive framing, and check whether the response would change if the same mistake were your own.
Standard Enforcement.oppositeDefinition: Compassionate standards: holding a real standard for work or conduct while separating a shortfall from a judgment of the other person's character, correcting without punishing, and applying the same standard to oneself that is being asked of others.

Imposture.def: A standing belief that one is fundamentally flawed or not genuinely competent, defended by hiding the belief itself: concealing the parts of oneself or one's history thought to reveal the flaw, and relocating responsibility when the concealment is challenged, rather than letting the belief or the evidence against it surface.
Imposture.body: Imposter supplies the core belief: a felt sense of fraudulence that persists even against real, visible evidence of competence. Overthinker supplies sustained, unresolved rumination on the gap between the felt fraudulence and the evidence against it, rather than a rumination that converges on relief. Deflector supplies the behavioral defense once the concealment is at risk of exposure: relocating responsibility or attention away from the thing being hidden, rather than letting it surface. Canon's own phrase, 'defectiveness schema plus a coping loop of hiding,' names this precisely: a belief (Defectiveness/Shame) paired with one specific coping strategy for it (avoidance, through concealment) rather than the belief alone.
Imposture.inferenceBasis: The name, saboteur triad and schema-domain placement are canon.json's own system-inferred entry (tag I), not owner dictation and not my own invention. The behavioral template below draws on three separately real literatures: Young's Defectiveness/Shame schema and its avoidance coping style, Clance and Imes's impostor phenomenon (a much more directly on-point use of that construct than its earlier use for a different complex elsewhere in this series, since this complex's own name and shame-based framing is what the construct actually describes), and real experimental research on shame-driven concealment specifically.
Imposture.behavior: May persist in feeling fraudulent or fundamentally inadequate despite direct, visible evidence of competence, think about the gap between that feeling and the evidence repeatedly without it resolving into relief, and actively hide the specific experiences, histories or feelings thought to reveal the flaw, deflecting or changing the subject when a conversation approaches them.
Imposture.triggerMechanism: Success, praise, or direct evidence of competence can activate doubt about whether it was earned rather than settle the underlying belief. A conversation or situation that risks surfacing the concealed material can activate deflection -- changing the subject, minimizing, or redirecting attention elsewhere -- rather than disclosure.
Imposture.livedExample: Praised for a piece of work, the person privately attributes it to luck or to others' low standards rather than to their own ability, turning the discrepancy over repeatedly afterward. When a conversation moves toward the specific experience or history behind the feeling of fraudulence, the person changes the subject or minimizes it rather than naming it.
Imposture.impact: Real evidence of competence does not update the underlying belief, so the person's own sense of their worth stays disconnected from their actual record. Concealment prevents the kind of disclosure that research on secrecy links to relief, so the belief and the isolation around it tend to persist together rather than resolve.
Imposture.practice: Keep a written, specific record of actual accomplishments to check against the felt sense of fraudulence, rather than relying on the feeling to update itself. Disclose the concealed material to one trusted person as a deliberate test of whether the feared exposure is as costly as it feels. Notice the pull to change the subject as a signal of what is being protected, not only as a conversational habit.
Imposture.oppositeDefinition: Owned competence: holding an account of one's own worth and ability that updates on real evidence, and disclosing rather than concealing the experiences thought to reveal a flaw, to at least one trusted person.
